claim: The basal ganglia have been implicated in monitoring of supra-second intervals.
source: Although the basal ganglia and cerebellum have been implicated in monitoring of supra- and sub-second intervals, respectively, the underlying neuronal mechanism remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established scientific literature on the functional roles of the basal ganglia.

claim: The cerebellum has been implicated in monitoring of sub-second intervals.
source: Although the basal ganglia and cerebellum have been implicated in monitoring of supra- and sub-second intervals, respectively, the underlying neuronal mechanism remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established scientific literature on the functional roles of the cerebellum.

claim: Neurons in the caudate nucleus kept track of passage of time throughout the delay period in monkeys trained to generate self-initiated saccades at instructed timing.
source: Here, we show that in monkeys trained to generate a self-initiated saccade at instructed timing following a visual cue, neurons in the caudate nucleus kept track of passage of time throughout the delay period, while those in the cerebellar dentate nucleus were recruited only during the last part of the delay period.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from neuronal recordings in monkeys performing the self-timed saccade task.

claim: Neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus were recruited only during the last part of the delay period in monkeys trained to generate self-initiated saccades at instructed timing.
source: Here, we show that in monkeys trained to generate a self-initiated saccade at instructed timing following a visual cue, neurons in the caudate nucleus kept track of passage of time throughout the delay period, while those in the cerebellar dentate nucleus were recruited only during the last part of the delay period.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from neuronal recordings in monkeys performing the self-timed saccade task.

claim: Neuronal correlates of trial-by-trial variation of self-timing emerged earlier in the cerebellum than the striatum.
source: Conversely, neuronal correlates of trial-by-trial variation of self-timing emerged earlier in the cerebellum than the striatum.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analyzing trial-by-trial variation in neuronal activity.

claim: Local inactivation of recording sites confirmed the difference in relative contributions of the caudate nucleus and cerebellar dentate nucleus to supra- and sub-second intervals.
source: Local inactivation of respective recording sites confirmed the difference in their relative contributions to supra- and sub-second intervals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from muscimol inactivation experiments.

claim: The basal ganglia may measure elapsed time relative to the intended interval.
source: These results suggest that the basal ganglia may measure elapsed time relative to the intended interval, while the cerebellum might be responsible for the fine adjustment of self-timing.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing different time courses of neuronal activity in the basal ganglia.

claim: The cerebellum might be responsible for the fine adjustment of self-timing.
source: These results suggest that the basal ganglia may measure elapsed time relative to the intended interval, while the cerebellum might be responsible for the fine adjustment of self-timing.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing neuronal correlates of trial-by-trial variation emerging earlier in the cerebellum.

claim: Both the basal ganglia and the cerebellum are implicated in action timing.
source: Previous studies have shown that, in addition to the cerebral cortex, both the basal ganglia and the cerebellum are implicated in this function (Buhusi and Meck, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In humans, the underlying neural mechanism of self-timing has been examined by recording scalp potentials that develop gradually over the medial frontal cortex in anticipation of task-relevant events.
source: In humans, the underlying neural mechanism of self-timing has been examined by recording scalp potentials that develop gradually over the medial frontal cortex in anticipation of task-relevant events (contingent negative variation or CNV: Macar and Vidal, 2003; van Rijn et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous human studies.

claim: CNV sometimes provides only a poor indication of event timing.
source: However, CNV sometimes provides only a poor indication of event timing (Kononowicz and van Rijn, 2011), possibly because it contains multiple components.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The magnitudes of CNV are correlated with neural activity in the thalamus, the basal ganglia, and the cerebellum.
source: In fact, the magnitudes of CNV are known to be correlated with neural activity in the thalamus, the basal ganglia, and the cerebellum (Nagai et al., 2004), indicating that the ramping-up of neuronal activity in the cerebral cortex is likely to be regulated by different signals arising from multiple subcortical structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The ramping-up of neuronal activity in the cerebral cortex is likely to be regulated by different signals arising from multiple subcortical structures.
source: In fact, the magnitudes of CNV are known to be correlated with neural activity in the thalamus, the basal ganglia, and the cerebellum (Nagai et al., 2004), indicating that the ramping-up of neuronal activity in the cerebral cortex is likely to be regulated by different signals arising from multiple subcortical structures.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation between CNV and subcortical activity.

claim: In monkeys, neurons in the motor thalamus exhibit a gradual rise in firing rate that predicts the timing of self-initiated movements.
source: In monkeys, neurons in the motor thalamus exhibit a gradual rise in firing rate that predicts the timing of self-initiated movements (Costello et al., 2016; Tanaka, 2007), and their inactivation causes delayed self-timing (Tanaka, 2006; van Donkelaar et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research in monkeys.

claim: Inactivation of motor thalamus neurons causes delayed self-timing in monkeys.
source: In monkeys, neurons in the motor thalamus exhibit a gradual rise in firing rate that predicts the timing of self-initiated movements (Costello et al., 2016; Tanaka, 2007), and their inactivation causes delayed self-timing (Tanaka, 2006; van Donkelaar et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous inactivation studies.

claim: Direct inputs from the thalamus are necessary for generating preparatory activity in the premotor cortex in rodents.
source: Recent studies in rodents have demonstrated that direct inputs from the thalamus are necessary for generating preparatory activity in the premotor cortex (Guo et al., 2017), while signals in the cortical network are also essential for generation (Murakami et al., 2014) and maintenance (Li et al., 2016) of ramping activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research in rodents.

claim: Signals in the cortical network are essential for generation of ramping activity.
source: Recent studies in rodents have demonstrated that direct inputs from the thalamus are necessary for generating preparatory activity in the premotor cortex (Guo et al., 2017), while signals in the cortical network are also essential for generation (Murakami et al., 2014) and maintenance (Li et al., 2016) of ramping activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Signals in the cortical network are essential for maintenance of ramping activity.
source: Recent studies in rodents have demonstrated that direct inputs from the thalamus are necessary for generating preparatory activity in the premotor cortex (Guo et al., 2017), while signals in the cortical network are also essential for generation (Murakami et al., 2014) and maintenance (Li et al., 2016) of ramping activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The thalamus transmits signals from both the basal ganglia and the cerebellum.
source: Because the thalamus transmits signals from both the basal ganglia and the cerebellum, elucidation of the neuronal activity in these subcortical structures will address specific roles of respective cortico-subcortical loops in self-timing.
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: A prevailing hypothesis is that the basal ganglia process supra-second interval timing while the cerebellum is involved in sub-second timing.
source: A prevailing hypothesis regarding subcortical contribution to timing is that the basal ganglia process supra-second interval timing while the cerebellum is involved in sub-second timing (Ivry and Spencer, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: Neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus exhibited preparatory activity only about a half second before self-initiated saccades, irrespective of the length of the mandatory delay interval that ranged from 400 to 2400 ms.
source: Our recent analysis in monkeys showed that neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus exhibited preparatory activity only about a half second before self-initiated saccades, irrespective of the length of the mandatory delay interval that ranged from 400 to 2400 ms (Ohmae et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: Neurons outside of the cerebellum must keep track of elapsed time to make temporally accurate movements in trials with supra-second delay intervals.
source: These results indicate that neurons outside of the cerebellum must keep track of elapsed time to make temporally accurate movements in trials with supra-second delay intervals.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that cerebellar neurons are recruited late.

claim: Neurons in the striatum are known to exhibit ramping activity during motor preparation.
source: Because neurons in the striatum are known to exhibit ramping activity during motor preparation (Schultz and Romo, 1992), signals in the cortico-basal ganglia loop might play this role.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Signals in the cortico-basal ganglia loop might play a role in keeping track of elapsed time for supra-second intervals.
source: Because neurons in the striatum are known to exhibit ramping activity during motor preparation (Schultz and Romo, 1992), signals in the cortico-basal ganglia loop might play this role.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from known striatal activity patterns.

claim: The anterior part of the striatum (caudate nucleus) and the posterior part of the cerebellar dentate nucleus have common anatomical connections with the medial and lateral frontal cortices involved in temporal processing.
source: Because the previous studies have demonstrated that these subcortical regions have common anatomical connections with the medial and lateral frontal cortices involved in temporal processing (Dum and Strick, 2003; Strick et al., 2009; McFarland and Haber, 2001), we reasoned that these areas might have functional interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The caudate nucleus and cerebellar dentate nucleus might have functional interactions.
source: Because the previous studies have demonstrated that these subcortical regions have common anatomical connections with the medial and lateral frontal cortices involved in temporal processing (Dum and Strick, 2003; Strick et al., 2009; McFarland and Haber, 2001), we reasoned that these areas might have functional interactions.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from anatomical connectivity.

claim: Plasticity in the cerebellar cortex rather than the deep cerebellar nuclei plays a role in the learning of motor timing in eye blink conditioning.
source: Although the previous studies of eye blink conditioning suggest that plasticity in the cerebellar cortex rather than the deep cerebellar nuclei plays a role in the learning of motor timing (Garcia and Mauk, 1998; Perrett et al., 1993; Raymond et al., 1996), neurons in the nuclei encode timing signals originated in the cerebellar cortex (Ten Brinke et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous eye blink conditioning studies.

claim: Neurons in the deep cerebellar nuclei encode timing signals originated in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Although the previous studies of eye blink conditioning suggest that plasticity in the cerebellar cortex rather than the deep cerebellar nuclei plays a role in the learning of motor timing (Garcia and Mauk, 1998; Perrett et al., 1993; Raymond et al., 1996), neurons in the nuclei encode timing signals originated in the cerebellar cortex (Ten Brinke et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Any significant computation in the lateral cerebellum must modify neuronal activity in the dentate nucleus that may eventually regulate movement timing.
source: Therefore, we explored signals in the dentate nucleus in this study because any significant computation in the lateral cerebellum must modify neuronal activity in the nucleus that may eventually regulate movement timing.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the known cerebellar circuitry.

claim: Neurons in the striatum displayed a ramping-up of firing rate throughout the delay period.
source: We found that neurons in the striatum displayed a ramping-up of firing rate throughout the delay period, while the rate of rise of neuronal activity depended on the length of the mandatory delay interval.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from neuronal recordings.

claim: The rate of rise of neuronal activity in the striatum depended on the length of the mandatory delay interval.
source: We found that neurons in the striatum displayed a ramping-up of firing rate throughout the delay period, while the rate of rise of neuronal activity depended on the length of the mandatory delay interval.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from neuronal recordings.

claim: Neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus exhibited preparatory activity only during the last part of the delay period.
source: In contrast, neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus exhibited preparatory activity only during the last part of the delay period, while neuronal correlates of trial-by-trial variation of saccade latency started earlier in the cerebellum than the striatum.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from neuronal recordings.

claim: Neuronal correlates of trial-by-trial variation of saccade latency started earlier in the cerebellum than the striatum.
source: In contrast, neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus exhibited preparatory activity only during the last part of the delay period, while neuronal correlates of trial-by-trial variation of saccade latency started earlier in the cerebellum than the striatum.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from neuronal recordings.

claim: The striatum may play a role in monitoring the passage of time relative to the mandatory interval.
source: These results suggest that the striatum may play a role in monitoring the passage of time relative to the mandatory interval, while the cerebellum might play a role in the fine adjustment of self-timing in the range of hundreds of milliseconds.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing scalable ramping activity in the striatum.

claim: The cerebellum might play a role in the fine adjustment of self-timing in the range of hundreds of milliseconds.
source: These results suggest that the striatum may play a role in monitoring the passage of time relative to the mandatory interval, while the cerebellum might play a role in the fine adjustment of self-timing in the range of hundreds of milliseconds.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing early trial-by-trial variation in the cerebellum.

claim: Both monkeys flexibly adjusted movement timing depending on the given instructions.
source: Distributions of saccade latency during recording sessions shown in Figure 1B (Figure 1—source data 1) indicate that both monkeys flexibly adjusted movement timing depending on the given instructions.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 162 task-related neurons were recorded in the anterior part of the caudate nucleus (63 and 99 neurons for monkeys B and G, respectively).
source: We recorded from 162 task-related neurons in the anterior part of the caudate nucleus (63 and 99 neurons for monkeys B and G, respectively) and 127 neurons in the posterior part of the cerebellar dentate nucleus (59 and 68, respectively, Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data on the number of recorded neurons.

claim: 127 task-related neurons were recorded in the posterior part of the cerebellar dentate nucleus (59 and 68 neurons for monkeys B and G, respectively).
source: We recorded from 162 task-related neurons in the anterior part of the caudate nucleus (63 and 99 neurons for monkeys B and G, respectively) and 127 neurons in the posterior part of the cerebellar dentate nucleus (59 and 68, respectively, Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data on the number of recorded neurons.

claim: 100 striatal neurons showed elevated activity before self-timed saccades (37 and 63 neurons for monkeys B and G, respectively).
source: Of these, 100 striatal neurons (37 and 63 neurons for monkeys B and G, respectively) and 76 cerebellar neurons (29 and 47 neurons) showed elevated activity before self-timed saccades (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data on neuronal activity.

claim: 76 cerebellar neurons showed elevated activity before self-timed saccades (29 and 47 neurons for monkeys B and G, respectively).
source: Of these, 100 striatal neurons (37 and 63 neurons for monkeys B and G, respectively) and 76 cerebellar neurons (29 and 47 neurons) showed elevated activity before self-timed saccades (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data on neuronal activity.

claim: Most neurons in the caudate nucleus exhibited increased activity for both saccade directions (55%).
source: Most of them exhibited increased activity for both saccade directions (55 and 66% for neuron in the caudate nucleus and the cerebellar dentate nucleus, respectively), while many showed a significant directional modulation (48/100 and 32/76, respectively; Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data on neuronal activity patterns.

claim: Most neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus exhibited increased activity for both saccade directions (66%).
source: Most of them exhibited increased activity for both saccade directions (55 and 66% for neuron in the caudate nucleus and the cerebellar dentate nucleus, respectively), while many showed a significant directional modulation (48/100 and 32/76, respectively; Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data on neuronal activity patterns.

claim: 48 out of 100 caudate neurons showed a significant directional modulation.
source: Most of them exhibited increased activity for both saccade directions (55 and 66% for neuron in the caudate nucleus and the cerebellar dentate nucleus, respectively), while many showed a significant directional modulation (48/100 and 32/76, respectively; Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: 32 out of 76 cerebellar dentate neurons showed a significant directional modulation.
source: Most of them exhibited increased activity for both saccade directions (55 and 66% for neuron in the caudate nucleus and the cerebellar dentate nucleus, respectively), while many showed a significant directional modulation (48/100 and 32/76, respectively; Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: A representative caudate neuron exhibited a gradual ramp-up of firing rate before self-timed saccades for all three mandatory delay intervals.
source: Figure 3A shows a representative example of caudate neuron exhibiting a gradual ramp-up of firing rate before self-timed saccades for all three mandatory delay intervals.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The rate of rise of firing rate differed for different interval timing in a representative caudate neuron.
source: This neuron elevated activity immediately after cue appearance but the rate of rise of firing rate differed for different interval timing.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the representative neuron shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A representative cerebellar nuclear neuron exhibited a ramp-up activity where the timing of ramp onset differed depending on the mandatory intervals.
source: In contrast, the representative cerebellar nuclear neuron shown in Figure 3B also exhibited a ramp-up activity, but the timing of ramp onset differed depending on the mandatory intervals, while the rate of rise of activity was roughly constant.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The rate of rise of activity was roughly constant across different mandatory intervals in a representative cerebellar nuclear neuron.
source: In contrast, the representative cerebellar nuclear neuron shown in Figure 3B also exhibited a ramp-up activity, but the timing of ramp onset differed depending on the mandatory intervals, while the rate of rise of activity was roughly constant.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the representative neuron shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The ramp-up activity started just after cue onset in the striatum population.
source: Again, the ramp-up activity started just after cue onset in the striatum (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1), while the firing modulation started late for trials with longer delay in the cerebellum (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by population data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The firing modulation started late for trials with longer delay in the cerebellum population.
source: Again, the ramp-up activity started just after cue onset in the striatum (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1), while the firing modulation started late for trials with longer delay in the cerebellum (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by population data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The rate of rise of preparatory activity differed for different interval timing in the caudate nucleus population.
source: The rate of rise of preparatory activity differed for different interval timing in the caudate nucleus (Figure 3C), while the activity was similar across all timing in the cerebellar dentate nucleus (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by population data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The activity was similar across all timing in the cerebellar dentate nucleus population.
source: The rate of rise of preparatory activity differed for different interval timing in the caudate nucleus (Figure 3C), while the activity was similar across all timing in the cerebellar dentate nucleus (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by population data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The time courses of individual neuronal activity during the delay interval were more variable in the striatum than the cerebellum.
source: In general, the time courses of individual neuronal activity during the delay interval were more variable in the striatum than the cerebellum (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neurons in both structures did not show clear ramping activity during the standard memory-guided saccade task.
source: Neurons in both structures did not show clear ramping activity during the standard memory-guided saccade task, in which animals generated a saccade in response to the FP offset (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: For all iterations (n = 1000) of bootstrap resampling, coefficients of determination (r2) of fitting were greater than 0.86.
source: For all iterations (n = 1000), coefficients of determination (r2) of fitting were greater than 0.86, and averaged 0.96 ± 0.01 (SD) for both structures.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of the fitting procedure.

claim: The times of ramp onset differed significantly between neurons in the striatum and those in the cerebellum for medium and long delay intervals.
source: Except for the shortest delay interval, the times of ramp onset differed significantly between neurons in the striatum and those in the cerebellum (p<0.05, bootstrap CIs).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using bootstrap confidence intervals.

claim: The slopes of ramp-up activity differed among the mandatory delay intervals for neurons in both the striatum and cerebellum.
source: Although the slopes differed among the mandatory delay intervals for neurons in both the striatum and cerebellum (one-way ANOVA, p<0.05), the difference was much greater in the striatum.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using one-way ANOVA.

claim: The difference in slopes of ramp-up activity among mandatory delay intervals was much greater in the striatum than the cerebellum.
source: Although the slopes differed among the mandatory delay intervals for neurons in both the striatum and cerebellum (one-way ANOVA, p<0.05), the difference was much greater in the striatum.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of statistical results between the two structures.

claim: The slopes for the medium and long delay conditions showed a significant difference between neurons in the striatum and those in the cerebellum.
source: Consistent with the results of ramp onset, the slopes for the medium and long delay conditions again showed a significant difference between neurons in the striatum and those in the cerebellum (p<0.05, bootstrap CIs).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using bootstrap confidence intervals.

claim: While striatal neurons were active throughout the delay period, dentate nuclear neurons were recruited only during the last part of the delay period in the self-timed task.
source: Thus, while striatal neurons were active throughout the delay period, dentate nuclear neurons were recruited only during the last part of the delay period in the self-timed task.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings from neuronal recordings and analysis.

claim: For neurons in the striatum, preparatory activity started immediately after cue onset, but trial-by-trial variation was evident only during the very last part of the delay interval.
source: For neurons in the striatum, preparatory activity started immediately after cue onset, but trial-by-trial variation was evident only during the very last part of the delay interval (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: For neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus, trial-by-trial variation started at the beginning of the preparatory activity except for trials with the shortest delay interval.
source: In contrast, for neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus, trial-by-trial variation started at the beginning of the preparatory activity except for trials with the shortest delay interval (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The baseline fluctuation (SD) of normalized neuronal activity was comparable between the recording sites.
source: The baseline fluctuation (SD) of normalized neuronal activity was comparable between the recording sites (unpaired t-test, p=0.84).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison using unpaired t-test.

claim: The trial-by-trial variation of neuronal activity started earlier in the cerebellum than the striatum for medium and long intervals.
source: The trial-by-trial variation of neuronal activity started earlier in the cerebellum than the striatum except for trials with the shortest mandatory delay interval (p<0.05, bootstrap CIs).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using bootstrap confidence intervals.

claim: The cerebellum might be primarily responsible for the fine adjustment of self-timing.
source: These results suggest that the cerebellum might be primarily responsible for the fine adjustment of self-timing, while the striatum may continuously monitor the time relative to the intended interval during the delay period.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on trial-by-trial variation.

claim: The striatum may continuously monitor the time relative to the intended interval during the delay period.
source: These results suggest that the cerebellum might be primarily responsible for the fine adjustment of self-timing, while the striatum may continuously monitor the time relative to the intended interval during the delay period.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on neuronal activity patterns.

claim: Some neurons in the basal ganglia and the cerebral cortex might be tuned to specific interval timing.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that some neurons in the basal ganglia and the cerebral cortex might be tuned to specific interval timing (Bartolo et al., 2014; Hayashi et al., 2015; Merchant et al., 2013b; Mita et al., 2009; Murakami et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A subset of caudate neurons showed a preference for specific mandatory delay interval.
source: Indeed, we found that a subset of caudate neurons showed a preference for specific mandatory delay interval, although the population activity at the time of saccade initiation was roughly the same across intervals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The population activity at the time of saccade initiation was roughly the same across intervals in the caudate nucleus.
source: Indeed, we found that a subset of caudate neurons showed a preference for specific mandatory delay interval, although the population activity at the time of saccade initiation was roughly the same across intervals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Among 31 (31%) caudate neurons exhibiting a significant duration selectivity, 18, 8, and five neurons showed a preference for short, medium, and long delay intervals, respectively.
source: Among 31 (31%) caudate neurons exhibiting a significant duration selectivity (one-way ANOVA, p<0.01), 18, 8, and five neurons showed a preference for short, medium, and long delay intervals, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: A smaller population of neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus (11/77, 14%) showed significant duration selectivity, with a preference for short, medium, and long intervals in 1, 8, and two neurons, respectively.
source: In contrast, a smaller population of neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus (11/77, 14%) showed significant duration selectivity, with a preference for short, medium, and long intervals in 1, 8, and two neurons, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: No topographic organization of neurons with or without duration selectivity was found in both structures.
source: In both structures, we found no topographic organization of neurons with or without duration selectivity.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the spatial distribution of recorded neurons.

claim: Striatal neurons tend to have greater duration selectivity than neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus.
source: The graph clearly shows that striatal neurons tend to have greater duration selectivity than neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test; contra, p=7.7E-11; ipsi, p=5.3E-12), whereas no obvious preference for a specific duration was found in the population of neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.

claim: No obvious preference for a specific duration was found in the population of neurons in either structure.
source: The graph clearly shows that striatal neurons tend to have greater duration selectivity than neurons in the cerebellar dentate nucleus (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test; contra, p=7.7E-11; ipsi, p=5.3E-12), whereas no obvious preference for a specific duration was found in the population of neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of population data shown in figures.

claim: During inactivation of the caudate nucleus, contraversive self-timed saccades were delayed in trials with short (400 ms) and long (2200 ms) mandatory delay intervals in a single experimental session.
source: During inactivation, contraversive self-timed saccades were delayed in trials with short (400 ms) and long (2200 ms) mandatory delay intervals (Wilcoxon rank-sum test; short, p=7.4E-3; long, p=4.8E-3), while ipsiversive saccades were facilitated for all delay intervals (short, p=4.5E-3; medium, p=1.2E-7; long, p=2.0E-4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a single inactivation session with statistical testing.

claim: During inactivation of the caudate nucleus, ipsiversive saccades were facilitated for all delay intervals in a single experimental session.
source: During inactivation, contraversive self-timed saccades were delayed in trials with short (400 ms) and long (2200 ms) mandatory delay intervals (Wilcoxon rank-sum test; short, p=7.4E-3; long, p=4.8E-3), while ipsiversive saccades were facilitated for all delay intervals (short, p=4.5E-3; medium, p=1.2E-7; long, p=2.0E-4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a single inactivation session with statistical testing.

claim: Among six experiments in the caudate nucleus, contraversive saccades were significantly delayed in three experiments.
source: Among six experiments (three experiments for each monkey), contraversive saccades were significantly delayed in three experiments, while ipsiversive saccades were significantly facilitated in four experiments (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05 with Bonferroni correction).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from multiple inactivation experiments.

claim: Among six experiments in the caudate nucleus, ipsiversive saccades were significantly facilitated in four experiments.
source: Among six experiments (three experiments for each monkey), contraversive saccades were significantly delayed in three experiments, while ipsiversive saccades were significantly facilitated in four experiments (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05 with Bonferroni correction).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from multiple inactivation experiments.

claim: In the population as a whole, the delay of contraversive self-timed saccades during caudate inactivation was found only in trials with a long delay interval.
source: In the population as a whole, the delay of contraversive self-timed saccades was found only in trials with a long delay interval (Figure 7C, paired t-test, p=0.038, Figure 7—source data 1), while the facilitation of ipsiversive saccades was consistently observed for all delay intervals (short, p=0.044; medium, p=0.048; long, p=0.021).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of population data using paired t-test.

claim: The facilitation of ipsiversive saccades during caudate inactivation was consistently observed for all delay intervals.
source: In the population as a whole, the delay of contraversive self-timed saccades was found only in trials with a long delay interval (Figure 7C, paired t-test, p=0.038, Figure 7—source data 1), while the facilitation of ipsiversive saccades was consistently observed for all delay intervals (short, p=0.044; medium, p=0.048; long, p=0.021).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of population data using paired t-test.

claim: A significant change in contraversive saccade latency was found in the standard memory-guided saccade trials during caudate inactivation.
source: We also found a significant change in contraversive saccade latency in the standard memory-guided saccade trials (paired t-test, p=0.012), but neither ipsiversive memory-guided saccades nor visually-guided saccades in both directions were altered during inactivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using paired t-test.

claim: Neither ipsiversive memory-guided saccades nor visually-guided saccades in both directions were altered during caudate inactivation.
source: We also found a significant change in contraversive saccade latency in the standard memory-guided saccade trials (paired t-test, p=0.012), but neither ipsiversive memory-guided saccades nor visually-guided saccades in both directions were altered during inactivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant changes.

claim: The variation of saccade latency remained unchanged in all conditions during caudate inactivation in the population.
